issues.legal_issue: A state law providing for compulsory acquisition of an estate falls within the State Legislature’s acquisition power rather than its power over succession.
material_facts: The challenged law provided for an estate to vest in the government following notification and for compensation to be apportioned among persons interested in it.
The challenge argued that the law altered joint-family rights and therefore concerned succession.
issues.conclusion: The law was within the State Legislature’s legislative competence because it concerned compulsory acquisition of land, not succession.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Government of India Act, 1935, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 9, compulsory acquisition of land was within the State Legislature’s competence. The law did not deal with succession under List III, Entry 7. The Court did not rely on any earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.state_law_competence_challenge: A party challenges the legislative competence of a state law in a proceeding concerning acquisition of an estate.
predicates.law_compulsorily_acquires_land: The state law provides for the compulsory transfer of land to the government.

issues.definition: When a state law is challenged for lack of competence and it provides for compulsory acquisition of land, the law is within the State Legislature’s competence.

issues.legal_issue: A law protected by its inclusion in the Ninth Schedule cannot be invalidated on the ground that it violates the right to equality.
material_facts: The challenged law was included in the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution.
The challenge alleged that the law discriminated between maintenance-holders and the principal landholder’s family members in distributing compensation.
issues.conclusion: The challenge under Article 14 was unavailable because Article 31B protected the law from invalidation on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31B provides that an Act included in the Ninth Schedule, or its provisions, is not to be deemed void for taking away or abridging rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution. Article 14 is in Part III. The law was listed in the Ninth Schedule. The Court did not rely on any earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.equality_challenge_to_law: A party challenges a law on the ground that it treats persons unequally.
predicates.law_in_ninth_schedule: The challenged law is included in the constitutional schedule that protects listed laws from certain fundamental-rights challenges.

issues.definition: An equality challenge to a law is barred when the challenged law is included in the protected constitutional schedule.

issues.legal_issue: For apportionment of advance compensation under the governing acquisition law, only persons within the statutory definition of sharers may claim compensation as sharers, and the court need not decide whether the estate’s impartible character changed after vesting.
material_facts: The proceeding concerned the distribution of advance compensation and interim payments following the estate’s vesting in the government.
The appellants claimed compensation as sharers on the basis that the estate’s impartible character ceased or its partible character revived upon vesting.
The governing law defined sharers by reference to the principal landholder and specified descendants in the male line living or in the womb on the notified date, including qualifying adoptees.
The appellants did not fall within that statutory definition.
issues.conclusion: The appellants could not receive compensation as sharers. The Court did not decide whether the estate’s impartible character ceased after the notified date; the appellants’ rights to the payments at issue were determined under the governing law.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(b), 3(c), 3(e) and 3(g) provide for vesting, the cessation of specified rights, and entitlement thereafter only to rights recognized or conferred by the Act. Section 45(2) defines the persons treated as sharers for apportionment. Sections 42 to 46 apply to advance compensation through section 54-A(4). The Court did not rely on any earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.advance_compensation_apportionment: The proceeding concerns apportionment of advance compensation or related interim payments after an estate is acquired.
predicates.estate_vested_in_government: The estate was transferred to and vested in the government under the acquisition law.
predicates.claimant_outside_statutory_sharer_group: The claimant is not among the persons identified by the governing law as sharers for compensation apportionment.

issues.definition: In an advance-compensation apportionment proceeding, a claimant outside the statutory sharer group is not entitled to compensation as a sharer after the estate vests in the government.

issues.legal_issue: An allowance payable to family members under an arrangement concerning an impartible estate is maintenance rather than a debt merely because the arrangement calls it an allowance.
material_facts: A family arrangement provided for recurring payments to the holder’s brothers and their male descendants while the estate remained with the holder’s line.
The payments were not stated to repay loans or other advances, and their duration depended on the continuation of male members in the relevant branches.
The arrangement treated payments to widows as maintenance and provided that they could receive amounts from the same branch allowance in specified circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The recipients were maintenance-holders, not creditors, notwithstanding the terminology used in the earlier document.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 42 and 45 distinguish claims for maintenance from claims by creditors, and section 45(2)(b) includes persons entitled to maintenance under a binding instrument or family arrangement. The character of a payment depends on its substance and basis, not simply on the label used for it. The Court did not rely on any earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.estate_compensation_claim: A person claims a share of compensation arising from the acquisition of an estate.
predicates.recurring_family_payment: A family arrangement provides recurring payments to family members from the estate or its income.
predicates.payment_not_given_for_debt: The payments were not made in repayment of a loan or other debt and were provided for the recipients’ support.

issues.definition: A recipient of recurring family payments for support, rather than repayment of a debt, is a maintenance-holder for purposes of an estate-compensation claim.

issues.legal_issue: Government liabilities chargeable to the estate must be deducted before compensation is apportioned among persons interested in the estate.
material_facts: The estate owed the government an amount payable from the estate’s income.
The government deducted part of that liability from the estimated compensation before depositing advance compensation.
The appellants argued that the maintenance share should be calculated on the compensation before that deduction.
issues.conclusion: The distributable compensation was the net amount after permissible government liabilities, including the estate’s government dues, had been deducted; the maintenance share was to be calculated on that net amount.
issues.legal_principle: Section 54-A(2) permits deduction of a specified portion of government dues from the advance deposit, and section 54-A(4) applies sections 42 to 46 to apportion the deposit. Section 41(1) and its proviso concern liabilities due to the government. Compensation available for distribution is the value of the estate less its liabilities, rather than a theoretical gross amount. The Court did not rely on any earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.advance_compensation_apportionment: The proceeding concerns apportionment of advance compensation for an acquired estate.
predicates.estate_has_government_liability: The estate owed a liability to the government chargeable against the estate.
predicates.liability_deducted_from_deposit: The government deducted a legally permissible part of the estate’s liability before depositing the advance compensation.

issues.definition: When an estate has a government liability that is permissibly deducted from the advance deposit, the compensation to be apportioned is the net amount after that deduction.

issues.legal_issue: The share of maintenance-holders in compensation is governed by the statutory cap and factors for apportionment, not by comparing an earlier allowance with the estate’s historical income.
material_facts: The governing law limited the portion of the remainder payable to maintenance-holders, after determining creditors’ claims, to one-fifth, subject to a specified exception.
The law directed the tribunal to consider matters including the compensation payable, the number of persons to be maintained, relationship, other income and family circumstances.
The earlier family arrangement fixed allowances after considering status and other relevant matters, not as a stated proportion of the estate’s income.
The appellants sought to calculate compensation by applying the proportion that an earlier allowance bore to the estate’s income at the time the allowance was fixed.
issues.conclusion: The statutory proportion and apportionment provisions governed the distribution, and the tribunal was not required to calculate a maintenance-holder’s compensation by reference to the historical ratio between the earlier allowance and the estate’s income.
issues.legal_principle: Section 45(3) provides for payment of qualifying creditors from the aggregate compensation before distribution of the remainder. Section 45(4) limits the maintenance-holders’ portion of that remainder, subject to its stated exception. Section 45(5) specifies the considerations for determining and apportioning that portion and permits reopening an existing maintenance arrangement when necessary. Sections 42 to 46 apply to advance compensation through section 54-A(4). The Court did not rely on any earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.maintenance_compensation_apportionment: The proceeding concerns apportionment of compensation among persons entitled to maintenance from an acquired estate.
predicates.statutory_cap_applies: The governing law limits the maintenance-holders’ collective share of the remainder after creditors’ claims are determined.
predicates.claimant_seeks_historical_income_ratio: A claimant seeks to calculate the present compensation share by comparing an earlier allowance with the estate’s income when that allowance was fixed.

issues.definition: When a statutory cap governs maintenance compensation, a claimant seeking to use an earlier allowance-to-income ratio is not entitled to have that historical ratio determine the apportionment.
